briefdescription.para: Public name of the formatter used to report operand values.

detaileddescription.para: The function comparators and the custom operators report the values of their operands when a check fails. Values of user-defined types can be reported only if the application provides an operator<< that writes them to this formatter, declared in the namespace of the type, so that it is found by argument-dependent lookup:

Without such an operator, comparators such as eq() do not compile for user-defined types, since the operand values cannot be formatted; only the scoped enumerations are formatted without it, by their underlying value. Plain boolean checks, such as expect (a == b), do not need it, but they report only the source location on failure. The same operator also writes the values appended to the messages of the checks (expect (a == b) << "a is " << a).
Applications use the operator<< overloads, and str() to test their own operators; the functions that manage the buffer are private to the framework.

briefdescription.para: Approximate equality comparator, with an explicit tolerance.

detaileddescription.para: The comparison succeeds if the distance between lhs and rhs is less than or equal to epsilon, so a tolerance of zero requires equal values. The operands are numbers, integral or floating-point, possibly of different types (the deprecated value wrappers and numeric literals are also accepted, and their own tolerance is not used). For the integers, the distance is computed exactly, also for operands of different signedness, so approx (0u, -1, 2) succeeds; for the other types, in their common floating-point type. A failure is reported as lhs ~ (rhs +/- epsilon).

The deprecated approx (value, epsilon) form, available only with MICRO_OS_PLUS_MICRO_TEST_PLUS_DEPRECATED_ENABLED, is a value wrapper instead, which applies its tolerance to the six comparisons and to the operators; it accepts only floating-point values.

6.0.0
The approx function template constructs a detail::approx_op from the forwarded operands and tolerance; the operands are numbers, so detail::as_operand(), which converts the C strings, is not needed.

The C strings (char arrays, including the string literals, and char pointers) are compared by content, also with std::string and std::string_view; a null char pointer is equal only to another null pointer. The other arrays (e.g. byte buffers) are compared element by element, also with a container, and written as ranges; the other pointers are compared by address. The pointers and arrays of char8_t, char16_t, char32_t, and wchar_t are not treated as strings: the arrays are compared element by element, including the terminating null character, and the pointers by address. The integers of different signedness are compared by value, as by std::cmp_equal(), not after the usual arithmetic conversions, so eq (-1, static_cast<unsigned> (-1)) fails.

Both operands must satisfy extension::printable, since they are reported on failure; an application type needs an operator<< for mt::expression_formatter, otherwise the call is rejected, with a diagnostic that names the operand type. The operands must also be comparable with the operator of the comparator, otherwise the call is rejected in the same way.
The same rules apply to ne(), gt(), ge(), lt(), and le().

A comparator object that evaluates to true if the operands are equal.
The eq function template provides a generic equality comparator for any types. The operands are first passed to detail::as_operand(), which converts the C strings to detail::c_string, and the other arrays to detail::array_operand, so that they are compared by content. It constructs a comparator object, with the detail::equal_to tag, which evaluates to true if the two values are equal, and which is reported with both values if not.
The operands are forwarded, so that the comparator moves the temporaries and refers to the named operands, without copying them.

briefdescription.para: Functions for comparing actual and expected values in tests.

detaileddescription.para: While any boolean expression can be used in expectations and requirements, dedicated comparator functions such as eq, ne, lt, le, gt, and ge provide enhanced reporting by explicitly showing the compared values when a check fails.
Using these comparators ensures that failed checks report both actual and expected values, making issues easier to diagnose.
Comparators are available for both fundamental types and standard containers. When a container comparison fails, the elements of both containers are shown.
If a comparator check fails, the output clearly indicates the actual and expected values:

The C strings (char arrays, including the string literals, and char pointers) are compared by content, also with std::string and std::string_view, so mt::eq (actual, "abc") checks the characters, not the addresses; a null char pointer is equal only to another null pointer (or nullptr), not to an empty string. The other arrays (including uint8_t buffers) are compared by content, element by element, also with a container; the other pointers are compared by address.

The operands must be comparable with the operator of the comparator; for example, mt::eq (a, b) does not compile when a == b would not. The comparison of integers of different signedness is made by value, as by std::cmp_equal(), so that mt::eq (-1, static_cast<unsigned> (-1)) fails, although -1 == static_cast<unsigned> (-1) is true.

Comparing Containers
Containers can be compared for equality or inequality using the same comparator functions. The comparison is performed with the == operator of the containers, so they must be of types that can be compared, usually of the same type. The standard == and != operators return a plain bool, so a failed check written with them could not show the elements. Only the first 16 elements of a container are shown; when two longer containers differ after them, the report adds the index of the first difference.
